extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and other patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate guidance from the Federal Circuit on applying 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice two-step) and § 112 (indefiniteness/Nautilus) in patent litigation, including standards for summary judgment, representative-claim treatment, and when underlying factual disputes preclude eligibility rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112 / Nautilus standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims, viewed in light of the specification and prosecution history, must 'inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.' (Nautilus, 134 S. Ct. at 2129).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claim terms in context of specification and prosecution history to determine whether they provide objective boundaries for those of skill in the art. A lack of definiteness renders claims invalid. Terms of degree can be definite if they 'provide enough certainty to one of skill in the art when read in the context of the invention.' (Interval Licensing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intrinsic and extrinsic evidence for indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: If intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history) fails to supply an objective boundary, courts may consider extrinsic evidence (e.g., expert testimony) to determine definiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts may rely on expert declarations to resolve indefiniteness where intrinsic record is silent or ambiguous; subsidiary factual findings based on extrinsic evidence are reviewed for clear error on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective boundary requirement for terms of degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms of degree (e.g., 'minimal', 'substantial') are not per se indefinite, but the claims/specification/prosecution history must supply a point of comparison or objective baseline to interpret the degree term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification only shows extreme examples (e.g., no redundancy) but the claim contemplates some redundancy, and prosecution history does not explain 'how much' is permitted, the term may be indefinite (Sonix and Interval Licensing distinctions discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim treatment and waiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may treat a claim as representative when the patentee does not present meaningful argument for distinctive significance of limitations in other claims or parties agree to treat a claim as representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee who advances meaningful, distinct arguments regarding dependent-claim limitations (e.g., arguing that dependent claims add inventive concepts) preserves those arguments; a court should not treat an independent claim as representative where the patentee has preserved separate arguments for dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step patent-eligibility framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract idea). Step 2: if so, consider the claim elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., whether an 'inventive concept' exists). (Alice, Mayo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Step 1 to identify the abstract idea (e.g., collecting/recognizing/storing data, classifying and storing digital images). At Step 2, examine whether claim limitations amount to 'well-understood, routine, conventional' activity or instead add an inventive concept that improves computer functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea determination must focus on claimed improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid being 'abstract', claim limitations must be directed to a specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities rather than using computers as mere tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting an invention to a technological environment (e.g., parsing from source to object code) does not defeat abstractness absent evidence that the claimed steps improve computer functionality in some way (see Enfish, Visual Memory distinctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual nature of 'well-understood, routine, conventional' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim element or combination is well-understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan at the time of the patent is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this is a factual determination, it may preclude resolution on summary judgment if there is a genuine dispute of material fact. Such facts relevant to invalidity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for factual assertions tied to invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Any underlying factual issue that is pertinent to an invalidity conclusion (including whether something was well-understood, routine, and conventional) must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Microsoft v. i4i: clear and convincing standard applies to facts supporting invalidity. On summary judgment, absence of clear-and-convincing evidence or existence of material factual disputes may bar eligibility rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standards as applied to § 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional-circuit law governs non-patent questions (here, Seventh Circuit). Summary judgment reviewed de novo: appropriate only when no genuine dispute as to any material fact and movant entitled to judgment as a matter of law (Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though patent eligibility is ultimately a question of law reviewed de novo, it may contain underlying factual issues; when such factual disputes exist, summary judgment is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing mere prior-art disclosure from 'well-understood, routine, conventional'
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that an element is disclosed in prior art does not, by itself, mean it was well-understood, routine, and conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must look beyond mere availability in the prior art to determine whether the technique was conventional such that it supplies no inventive concept; this determination is fact-intensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: What can constitute an inventive concept under Alice step two
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that capture purported unconventional activities that improve computer functionality—e.g., 'storing a reconciled object structure in the archive without substantial redundancy' and 'selectively editing an object structure linked to other structures to thereby effect a one-to-many change'—may supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification and claims capture such improvements (and there is factual support), they can create a genuine issue of material fact about eligibility; summary judgment may be improper where these issues are disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of appellate review of mixed law/fact patent issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Review de novo for legal conclusions (e.g., ultimate § 101 determination), but underlying subsidiary factual findings are reviewed for clear error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts must respect district-court subsidiary fact findings (e.g., credibility of expert testimony) unless clearly erroneous; legal application of facts to law is reviewed de novo.
